title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre got out of his carriage and, passing the toiling militiamen, climbed the knoll from which, according to the doctor, the battlefield could be seen.
It was about eleven o'clock. The sun was somewhat to the left and behind him, and brightly illuminated the enormous panorama that rose like an amphitheater before him in the clear, thin air.

From the upper left, cutting through that amphitheater, wound the Smolensk highway, passing through a village with a white church about five hundred paces ahead of the knoll and below it. This was Borodino. Below the village the road crossed the river by a bridge and, winding down and up, rose higher and higher to the village of Valuevo, visible about four miles away, where Napoleon was then stationed. Beyond Valuevo the road vanished into a yellowing forest on the horizon. Far in the distance in that birch and fir forest to the right of the road, the cross and belfry of the Kolocha Monastery gleamed in the sun. Scattered over the whole blue expanse, to right and left of the forest and the road, smoking campfires could be seen and indistinct masses of troops—ours and the enemy's. The ground to the right—along the course of the Kolocha and Moskva rivers—was broken and hilly. Between the hollows, the villages of Bezubova and Zakharino were visible in the distance. On the left the ground was more level; there were grain fields, and the smoking ruins of Semenovsk, which had been burned, could be seen.

Everything Pierre saw was so indistinct that neither the left nor the right side of the field matched what he had expected. Nowhere could he see the battlefield he had imagined—only fields, meadows, troops, woods, campfire smoke, villages, hills, and streams; and try as he might, he could make out no military "position" in this place teeming with life, nor could he even tell our troops from the enemy's.
"I need to ask someone who knows," he thought, and approached an officer who was looking with curiosity at his huge, unmilitary figure.
"May I ask," said Pierre, "what village that is ahead?"
"Burdino, isn't it?" said the officer, turning to his companion.
"Borodino," the other corrected him.
The officer, clearly glad of a chance to talk, moved up to Pierre.
"Are those our men there?" Pierre asked.
"Yes, and farther on are the French," said the officer. "There they are, there... you can see them."
"Where? Where?" asked Pierre.
"You can see them with the naked eye... Look, there!"
The officer pointed toward the smoke visible to the left beyond the river, and the same stern and serious expression Pierre had noticed on many faces that day came over his own.
"Ah, those are the French! And over there?" Pierre pointed to a knoll on the left, near which some troops were visible.
"Those are ours."
"And there?" Pierre pointed to another knoll in the distance with a big tree on it, near a village in a hollow where campfires were smoking and something dark could be seen.
"That's his again," said the officer. (It was the Shevardino Redoubt.) "It was ours yesterday, but now it's his."
"Then where's our position?"

"Our position?" replied the officer with a satisfied smile. "I can tell you quite clearly, because I built nearly all our fortifications. There, you see? There's our center, at Borodino, right there," and he pointed to the village with the white church ahead. "That's where you cross the Kolocha. You see down there where the rows of hay are in the hollow? That's the bridge. That's our center. Our right flank is over there"—he pointed sharply to the right, far away in the broken ground—"that's where the Moskva River is, and we've built three very strong redoubts there. The left flank..." Here the officer paused. "Well, you see, that's harder to explain... Yesterday our left flank was there at Shevardino, you see, where the oak is, but now we've pulled our left wing back—now it's over there, do you see that village and the smoke? That's Semenovsk, yes, there," he pointed to Raevsky's knoll. "But the battle probably won't be there. His having moved his troops there is just a feint; he'll probably swing around to the right of the Moskva. But wherever it may be, many a man won't be here tomorrow!" he added.
An elderly sergeant who had come up while the officer was speaking had waited silently for him to finish, but at this point, evidently not liking the officer's remark, interrupted him.
"Gabions need to be sent for," he said sternly.
The officer looked embarrassed, as though he understood one might think about how many men would be missing tomorrow but shouldn't say it aloud.
"Well, send third company again," the officer said quickly.
"And you—are you one of the doctors?"
"No, I've come on my own," answered Pierre, and he went back down the hill, passing the militiamen.
"Oh, those damned fellows!" muttered the officer, following him and holding his nose as he ran past the working men.
"There they are... bringing her, coming... There they are... They'll be here in a minute..." voices were suddenly heard, and officers, soldiers, and militiamen began running forward along the road.
A church procession was coming up the hill from Borodino. First along the dusty road came infantry in ranks, bareheaded and with arms reversed. From behind them came the sound of church singing.
Soldiers and militiamen ran bareheaded past Pierre toward the procession.
"They're bringing her—our Protectress!... The Iberian Mother of God!" someone cried.
"The Smolensk Mother of God," another corrected him.

The militiamen—both those who had been in the village and those who had been working on the battery—threw down their shovels and ran to meet the church procession. Following the battalion that marched along the dusty road came priests in their vestments—one little old man in a hood with attendants and singers. Behind them, soldiers and officers carried a large, dark-faced icon in an embossed metal cover. This was the icon that had been brought from Smolensk and had since accompanied the army. Behind, before, and on both sides, crowds of militiamen with bared heads walked, ran, and bowed to the ground.

At the top of the hill they stopped with the icon; the men who had been holding it up by the linen bands were relieved by others, the chanters relit their censers, and the service began. The hot rays of the sun beat straight down, and a fresh soft wind played with the hair of the bared heads and with the ribbons decorating the icon. The singing didn't sound loud under the open sky. An immense crowd of bareheaded officers, soldiers, and militiamen surrounded the icon. Behind the priest and chanter stood the dignitaries in a reserved spot. A bald general with a Saint George's Cross on his neck stood just behind the priest, and without crossing himself (he was evidently a German) patiently waited for the service to end, which he considered it necessary to attend, probably to arouse the Russian people's patriotism. Another general stood in a martial pose, crossing himself with a quick motion of his hand before his chest while looking about him. Standing among the crowd of peasants, Pierre recognized several acquaintances among these notables but didn't look at them—his whole attention was absorbed by the serious expression on the faces of the soldiers and militiamen, who were all gazing intently at the icon. As soon as the tired chanters, who were singing the service for the twentieth time that day, began lazily and mechanically to sing, "Save from calamity Your servants, O Mother of God," and the priest and deacon chimed in, "For to You under God we all flee as to an unbreakable wall and protection," there again kindled in all those faces the same expression of awareness of the solemnity of the approaching moment that Pierre had seen at the foot of the hill at Mozhaysk and fleetingly on the many faces he had met that morning; and heads bowed more often, hair was tossed back, and sighs and the sound of men crossing themselves were heard.
The crowd around the icon suddenly parted and pressed against Pierre. Someone—a very important person, judging by the haste with which way was made—was approaching the icon.
It was Kutuzov, who had been riding around the position and on his way back to Tatarinova had stopped where the service was being held. Pierre recognized him at once by his distinctive figure.

With a long overcoat on his extremely stout, round-shouldered body, with his uncovered white head and puffy face showing the white ball of the eye he had lost, Kutuzov walked with a plunging, swaying gait into the crowd and stopped behind the priest. He crossed himself with a practiced movement, reached down and touched the ground with his hand, and bowed his white head with a deep sigh. Behind Kutuzov was Bennigsen and the suite. Despite the commander in chief's presence, which attracted the attention of all the senior officers, the militiamen and soldiers continued their prayers without looking at him.

When the service was over, Kutuzov stepped up to the icon, sank heavily to his knees, bowed to the ground, and for a long time tried in vain to rise but could not because of his weakness and weight. His white head twitched with the effort. At last he rose, kissed the icon as a child does with naively pouting lips, and again bowed until he touched the ground with his hand. The other generals followed his example, then the officers, and after them, with excited faces, pressing on one another, crowding, panting, and pushing, came the soldiers and militiamen.
